extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Plato/ancient philosophy; educators and scholars interested in classical theories of education and culture
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts of Plato (as reported by the commentator) prescribing standards for education, literature, music, gymnastic, and public morals in the ideal State, with examples and prohibitions drawn from Homeric poetry and traditional religion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship of nursery tales
rubrics_metrics.description: Children ought not to learn stories which they will have to unlearn; there must be a censorship of nursery tales, banishing some and keeping others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ban tales that are immoral or plainly false as education for the young (examples: Homer and Hesiod's accounts of Uranus, Saturn, Zeus inciting Pandarus, Hephaestus binding his mother). If tales are permitted, do so only under strict control (e.g., 'in a mystery' and only after appropriate rites).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of the gods — God as author of good only
rubrics_metrics.description: God must be represented as he is; not as the author of both good and evil or as causing men to sin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forbid poets who say God is 'the steward of good and evil' or that gods incited immoral acts or caused suffering (e.g., rejecting portrayals where God causes the Trojan war or the sufferings of Niobe). This is the 'first and great principle.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of the gods — God unchangeable and true
rubrics_metrics.description: God has no variableness or change of form; gods should not be depicted as disguising themselves or deceiving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ban poetic depictions of gods prowling about in strange disguises or using deceitful forms (the 'lying dream' or 'blasphemous nonsense' mothers tell children). Argument: the best (divine) nature is not liable to change or deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of falsehood in education — restricted 'economies'
rubrics_metrics.description: Falsehood (fiction) can be used as a pedagogical tool but must be restricted and used for good moral effect; dangerous weapon reserved to rulers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach children through imagination first and truth later; allow 'economies' only when required by human faculties or necessary for communicating knowledge, and only by those in authority. The common man must not be permitted to lie to the ruler.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ban on tales that promote fear of death
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove terrifying and discouraging portrayals of the underworld and ghosts from the education of soldiers and citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expunge passages that make death appear terrible or the underworld horrible (examples: lines where Achilles prefers servitude to ruling the dead, descriptions of Cocytus, Styx, 'sapless shades'). Rationale: courage requires not fearing death.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperance and avoidance of praise for gluttony/sexual excess
rubrics_metrics.description: Youth must be temperate; literature that praises eating, drinking, sexual license, or greed should be excluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forbid or excise verses that extol feasting, drunkenness, erotic exploits or encourage bribery and meanness (examples: Ionian/Lydian convivial strains in Homer; Phoenix advising Achilles to take gifts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of gods/heroic lamentation and excessive emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not teach or display weeping, frantic lamentation, or immoderate sorrow in tales for the guardians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude scenes where gods or heroes are reduced to tears, prostration, or senseless grief (examples: Achilles in tears, Priam rolling in the mire). Such examples encourage weakness and imitation among youth destined to be guardians.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic imitation restricted — prefer descriptive style
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal guardian should not be an imitator; the descriptive (narrative) style is preferred over dramatic imitation for formative education.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dramatic/imitative performance that requires playing many parts; guardians should not act women, slaves, bullies, cowards, drunkards, animals, etc., because 'the mask which the actor wears is apt to become his face.' If imitation is allowed, it must represent the good only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and moral appropriateness in poetry style and metre
rubrics_metrics.description: Style must conform to subject; metre and rhythm should be simple and suitable to the moral and psychological effect desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject complex, mixed forms attractive to youth; prefer simple metres and rhythms (ratios cited: 3/2, 2/2, 2/1) and align harmonic/metrical choices to the content (consult musician Damon for specifics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Purgation of music — permitted harmonies and instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain musical harmonies and instruments are suitable for cultivating temperance and courage; others are to be banned as corrupting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ban mixed Lydian and Ionian convivial harmonies (associated with lamentation or intemperance). Permit Dorian (martial/courage) and Phrygian (peace/obedience) harmonies; restrict instruments (ban complex many-stringed instruments and especially the flute; permit lyre and harp in town, Pan's pipe in fields).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculpture and painting must reflect simplicity and beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual arts should conform to the law of simplicity and avoid unseemliness or deformity that could corrupt taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prohibit art that depicts deformity or meanness which would 'poison and corrupt' the souls of guardians; cultivate a 'land of health and beauty' so citizens drink in harmonious influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of education: music before gymnastics; elements first
rubrics_metrics.description: Education should begin with music (including literature) then proceed to gymnastics; instruction should move from elemental forms to complex combinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach the elements (letters, basic musical forms, basic virtues) first, then show combinations and their reflections in life; the music of the soul precedes and prepares for reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gymnastics and regimen for guardians — simplicity and hardiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical training for guardians should favor simplicity, endurance, and abstention from excess (including strong drink), producing hardy, adaptable soldiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guardians should abstain from strong drink; prefer simpler gymnastic (not sleepy palaestra habits); diet guidelines modeled on Homeric heroes (roast meat only, no fish, no boiled meats, no sweet sauces). The aim is robustness, not luxury that breeds doctors and lawyers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid creating dependence on law and medicine through luxury
rubrics_metrics.description: A society that indulges luxury will generate needless lawyers and doctors; educational/cultural policy should prevent this by fostering simplicity and self-discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discourage habits (gluttony, luxury) that create demand for legal and medical specialization; arrange life so citizens have less need to resort to pleaders and physicians for problems of luxury and vice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral priority over historical truth in early religious education
rubrics_metrics.description: When teaching religion to the young, moral effect is primary; historical accuracy is secondary and may be disregarded if traditions are morally corrupting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the moral before the historical truth of religion for formative purposes; tolerate or reinterpret ancient religious errors rather than present them literally when they would corrupt youth.
